slides.0.title: Viticulture and Climate Change
slides.0.subtitle: Winter injury, vine burial and wind machines, wildfire smoke and extreme weather
slides.1.title: BC: the 2022–2024 cold events
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Late 2022 and 2023
slides.1.highlights.0.content: In December 2022 temperatures in the Similkameen Valley fell to -25°C, and BC's 2023 harvest was down about 58% (a survey had predicted 56%). Okanagan declines in 2023 by variety: Syrah 72%, Merlot 66% (the Okanagan's most planted), Cabernet Franc 47%, Chardonnay 47% and Riesling 41% (the hardiest); afterwards 29% of vineyards needed replanting (The Narwhal, Wine Anorak)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: January 2024
slides.1.highlights.1.content: In January 2024 temperatures in the Okanagan, Similkameen and Thompson valleys fell below -25°C after daytime highs of 10–13°C. Vines were near their maximum hardiness (about -22 to -24°C) but the drop was too rapid and extreme. Researchers dissected thousands of buds from 32 varieties in 9 regions and found no living buds, secondary buds included; the industry forecast a 97–99% loss for 2024 (The Narwhal, Wine Anorak)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Losses and aid
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Wine Growers BC estimated the January 2024 damage at CAD 440–445 million and replanting at CAD 162–317 million; in March 2024 the federal government announced CAD 177 million to extend the Wine Sector Support Program and BC announced CAD 70 million to expand the Perennial Crop Renewal Program (The Narwhal). These are press figures from a single source
slides.1.content: Cold injury is not only an eastern problem: BC can lose a whole crop in one winter.
slides.2.title: Ontario's cold injury and protection
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The winters of 2014–2015
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The 2014 "polar vortex" damaged Ontario's most fragile varieties widely; Brock University CCOVI sampling after the 2015 winter showed bud survival as low as Chardonnay 10% (Vinemount Ridge), Cabernet Franc 17% and Riesling 32%. Bud survival does not translate directly to crop: 60% bud survival is not a 60% crop (Wines in Niagara)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: What wind machines do
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Wind machines worked on calm, clear radiation-freeze nights with a good temperature inversion, and December and January data showed they reduced freeze injury; they were not useful during long, windy cold spells without an inversion (Wines in Niagara)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Burial, covers and hardy varieties
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Prince Edward County growers hill up vines after harvest; some Quebec wineries bury vines and increasingly use geotextile covers, and growers who do not bury must plant the hardiest hybrids; Quebec growers also helped develop thermal blankets tented over the rows (Wine With Seth, Luxe Magazine, Fine Vintage)
slides.2.content: The options: wind machines, burial, covers or hardier varieties.
slides.3.title: Wildfire smoke and climate change
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The 2018 study
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Wesley Zandberg's team at UBC Okanagan studied 10 Okanagan wines from the serious 2018 fire season: all were perceptibly influenced by smoke, three were marketed as "smoke affected" and seven were never sold because high smoke taint was detected after fermentation (UBC Okanagan)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Marker compounds
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Guaiacol and 4-methylguaiacol are the accepted markers of smoke taint; labs analysed these two accurately and consistently but were less accurate for other volatile phenols, especially free cresols, which correlated most strongly with the taste and smell of smoke taint. Sensory traits include cold ash, medicinal or burnt-rubber aromas and an ashy aftertaste (UBC Okanagan, Molecules)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Climate projections
slides.3.highlights.2.content: "Smoke-affected" and "smoke-tainted" differ: tainting depends on whether most people would enjoy the smoke character, and guaiacol can also rise after oak maturation. The Narwhal cites a 2016 study projecting by the 2050s a regional temperature 2.5°C above baseline and nearly seven times as many extremely hot days, a single-source claim; researchers also suggest testing heat-tolerant varieties from Spain, southern France and Greece
slides.3.content: Extreme cold and wildfire are opposite risks for Canadian viticulture.
